note.text: Some adverbs form comparisons irregularly. Well becomes better and best; badly becomes worse and worst. Far can become farther or further, depending on the use; course conventions should be stated. A comparative relates performances or situations; a superlative identifies the highest or lowest within a group in the relevant respect. Do not add more to better or attach -er to well. Distinguish the adjective good from the adverb well when describing how an action is performed.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: Some adverbs form comparisons irregularly. Well becomes better and best; badly becomes worse and worst. Far can become farther or further, depending on the use; course conventions should be stated. A comparative relates performances or situations; a superlative identifies the highest or lowest within a group in the relevant respect. Do not add more to better or attach -er to well. Distinguish the adjective good from the adverb well when describing how an action is performed.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: Bih reads well. After practice she reads better than before. In the stated group, she reads best. This compares a performance, not her worth as a person. A class should specify the comparison group and the criterion rather than treating best as a permanent label on a learner.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Find the verb being modified and the comparison intended. Use than when an explicit comparative clause needs it. Avoid double comparison such as more better. When several forms are standard, do not invent an incorrect rule just to force one option.
